title: Media coverage of COVID-19 health information in India: a content analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis of 2,422 COVID-19 articles from the websites of the five leading Indian national English-language newspapers (11 March - 30 April 2020), coded against WHO Strategic Risk Communications guidance and WHO's own COVID-19 updates. It reports quantitative shares of articles carrying misleading claims with stated denominators: '40% of media coverage of treatments options provided misleading information', 50/75 (66.7%) of chloroquine articles suggesting the drug may be effective and 43/64 (67.2%) of plasma-therapy articles suggesting that treatment was likely effective, all judged discordant with WHO guidance. Because falsity is judged against an external ground truth (WHO updates / guideline concordance explicitly labelled misleading), these are CONTENT rows, not QUALITY. The framework's other indicators (actionable, credible, understandable, timely) are quality/completeness measures and yield no prevalence rows.

estimates.platform: Online news websites of the five most-visited Indian national English-language newspapers (Times of India, The Hindu, Hindustan Times, The Indian Express, The Tribune)
estimates.measure_type: % of articles covering COVID-19 treatment options that provided misleading information
estimates.value_raw: 40% of media coverage of treatment options (denominator: the 314 articles that discussed COVID-19 treatments)
estimates.denominator: 314 articles (of 2,422 analysed) that discussed COVID-19 treatments and cures, from the five leading Indian national English-language newspaper websites, 11 Mar - 30 Apr 2020
estimates.definition: The article presented a treatment as effective when WHO had not established effectiveness - e.g. stating plasma therapy or chloroquine were effective; coded as 'misleading information' by the authors against the WHO COVID-19 update timeline
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper gives no formal definition of misinformation; the operational standard is discordance with WHO updates: "40% of media coverage of treatments options provided misleading information, such as suggesting plasma therapy or chloroquine, were effective"
estimates.source_quote: However, 40% of media coverage of treatments options provided misleading information, such as suggesting plasma therapy or chloroquine, were effective.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four coders analysed full texts in NVivo 12 against a timeline of WHO communications and the WHO Strategic Communications Framework indicators; 'All coders shared any new codes generated and discussed discrepancies to ensure concurrence on daily basis'. No inter-coder reliability statistic (kappa or percent agreement) is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The websites of the top five Indian national English newspapers were systematically searched. ... In all websites, either the archive of the dedicated 'Coronavirus' or 'COVID-19' sections were screened, or if this section was not present, website searches of two terms 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19' were conducted. ... we restricted searches to articles published between 11 March and 30 April. // Three hundred and fourteen articles discussed COVID-19 treatments.
estimates.notes: The 40% is stated verbatim ONLY in the Summary/abstract; the Results section never repeats it and does not show its derivation. It is close to the sum of the paper's own misleading-treatment counts (chloroquine 50 + plasma 43 + Ayurveda-as-immunity-booster 16 + yoga 14 = 123/314 = 39.2%), which suggests it is an author-computed cross-category total; kept under R8 because the authors state it verbatim, but confidence is medium and an adjudicator may prefer to rely on the two drug-specific rows instead. Denominator size taken from 'Three hundred and fourteen articles discussed COVID-19 treatments'; note the paper elsewhere miswrites this as 'these 324 articles' (75/314 = 23.9% confirms 314 is correct). denom_selection coded curated because the five outlets were rank-selected by website visitation (a purposive, mainstream-only frame that will understate misinformation relative to the wider Indian media, and excludes all non-English and print media); a reader could defensibly leave denom_selection blank since within those outlets all matching articles were taken. population_scope=other (news outlets, not people).

estimates.platform: Online news websites of the five most-visited Indian national English-language newspapers
estimates.measure_type: % of articles discussing chloroquine that suggested it may be effective against COVID-19, contrary to WHO's statement that there was no evidence of effectiveness in humans
estimates.denominator: 75 articles discussing chloroquine (23.9% of the 314 treatment articles)
estimates.definition: Article suggested chloroquine may be effective; WHO had stated only that it inhibits viral growth in laboratory studies with 'no evidence yet of effectiveness in humans', and 28 of these articles (37.3%) went further and suggested it could be taken as prophylaxis by high-risk individuals
estimates.misinfo_def: Operationalised as discordance with WHO guidance: "WHO stated that chloroquine had been shown to inhibit the growth of COVID-19 virus in laboratory studies, but there is no evidence yet of effectiveness in humans."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four coders, NVivo 12, content coded against a WHO-updates timeline; discrepancies discussed daily to reach concurrence; no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Seventy-five (23.9%) of these 324 [sic: 314] articles discussed chloroquine.
estimates.notes: Verbatim count and percentage, so kept under R8. The denominator is very narrow (articles that mention one drug), so this is a within-topic falsity rate, not a population prevalence; it should not be pooled with corpus-level shares. Codes are not mutually exclusive (35 said effectiveness unknown, 50 said it may be effective, 19 discussed side effects, 9 said use not recommended - these overlap within the same 75 articles), so an article could be counted in more than one category. The authors' own reading is that this coverage was misleading: 'There was significant coverage suggesting chloroquine was an effective prophylaxis, despite WHO's advice not to take it.' QUOTE NOTE: the text rendering interleaves the two printed columns, so no longer contiguous span is available; the full printed sentence is 'Of articles discussing chloroquine, only 35 (46.7%) identified that its effectiveness was unknown. However, 50 (66.7%) suggested that it may be effective, including 28 (37.3%) articles suggesting it could be taken as a preventive (prophylaxis) by high-risk individuals such as health workers.'

estimates.platform: Online news websites of the five most-visited Indian national English-language newspapers
estimates.measure_type: % of articles discussing plasma therapy that suggested the treatment was likely to be effective, which WHO had not verified
estimates.denominator: 64 articles discussing plasma therapy (20.4% of the 314 treatment articles)
estimates.definition: Article suggested plasma therapy was likely to be effective against COVID-19, a treatment 'not verified by WHO' and which the authors state 'should not be administered widely until its efficacy and safety have been established'
estimates.misinfo_def: Operationalised as discordance with WHO guidance; the paper's summary labels such coverage 'misleading information, such as suggesting plasma therapy or chloroquine, were effective'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four coders, NVivo 12, coded against WHO updates; daily discussion of discrepancies; no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Beyond those discussed by WHO, 314 articles covered a range of other treatments and cures. Plasma therapy was discussed in 64 (20.4%) of these.
estimates.notes: Verbatim count and percentage (R8 satisfied). Categories overlap - 43 (67.2%) said likely effective while 40 (62.5%) also noted it was unproven, so the same article can appear in both - meaning this is a share of articles CONTAINING a misleading claim, not a share of articles that are wholly misleading. Narrow, single-treatment denominator; not poolable with corpus-level prevalence. QUOTE NOTE: two-column interleaving again limits the contiguous span; the full printed sentence is 'From articles discussing plasma therapy, 43 (67.2%) suggested the treatment was likely to be effective, 40 (62.5%) noted that it had not been proven to be effective, and 11 (17.2%) stated that the treatment was not recommended.'

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) The WHO-framework indicators - 456/2,422 (18.8%) articles with actionable suggestions, 694 (28.7%) quoting identified sources, 464/694 (66.9%) using credible sources vs 541 (78.0%) non-credible, 86 (3.6%) using complicated language, 1.9% discussing equity - are completeness/quality indicators against a communication framework, not falsity judgements, so they are QUALITY-type coverage measures and generate no prevalence rows (a wholly accurate article can fail every one of them). (b) The many coverage counts (e.g. 735/1,065 articles on social distancing, 220 on masks, 254 on high-risk groups) are topic-coverage, not veracity. (c) Sub-claim falsity shares I judged too fine-grained under R4 but which an adjudicator might want: 2/8 (25.0%) of faeces-transmission articles suggested transmission may be possible despite WHO saying it does not occur; 16/24 (66.7%) of Ayurveda articles suggested Ayurveda was preventative as an immunity booster; 14 (4.5%) identified yoga as an immunity booster; 2/20 (10%) said we are immune after contracting COVID-19; 4/17 (23.5%) suggested spread is seasonal. These are single-claim denominators of 8-24 articles. (d) 'Twenty-one articles (6.7%) explicitly stated that no cure exists' - accurate coverage, the complement is not extractable (R8 bars complements). (e) The paper's internal inconsistency 'these 324 articles' vs 'Three hundred and fourteen articles discussed COVID-19 treatments' (75/314 = 23.9% confirms 314). (f) Percentages within the immunity/transmission sub-analyses sometimes sum to more than 100% (e.g. immunity: 65% + 40% + 10%), confirming non-exclusive multi-coding.

rob.design: Content analysis of online news. Frame: the websites of the top five Indian national English-language newspapers by website visitation (Times of India, The Hindu, Hindustan Times, The Indian Express, The Tribune); dedicated 'Coronavirus'/'COVID-19' archives screened, or site searches on 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19'; window 11 March - 30 April 2020. 3,507 titles retrieved, 1,085 excluded at full text (1,008 off-topic, 44 other-country only, 33 non-text/duplicate/out-of-range), 2,422 analysed. Coding: articles split between four coders in NVivo 12 against the WHO Strategic Communications Framework (five of six components) and a purpose-built timeline of WHO COVID-19 updates; new codes shared and discrepancies discussed daily 'to ensure concurrence'; NO double-coding of a reliability subsample and NO kappa or percent-agreement statistic is reported. Chi-squared tests (SPSS 25) for differences between proportions. Key weaknesses for prevalence use: English-language, online, national-newspaper-only frame (the authors note only ~39% of Indians read newspapers and that resource limits excluded print and other languages); denominators for the falsity shares are sub-topics chosen post hoc; the headline 40% appears only in the abstract with no shown derivation; coding categories are not mutually exclusive.
